<reason>Both sides were disciplined and grounded. B's central move—forcing the question of whether "expected to adopt" is a redundant social expectation or a formal gate that measurably restricts membership—structured the whole debate and never lost its grip. A attempted a third position (expectation as a membership standard that stops the host from making exit costless), which had real content, but B repeatedly reduced it to "naming" what opportunity already does, and A's answers grew more qualified over rounds. B answered A's sharpest pressure questions directly and with usable examples (Finland's Swedish institutions, multilingual ballots, the law/parallel-legal-codes distinction), while cleanly drawing the symmetry line that the same law binds native and newcomer. A's strongest material—the two-class public, the parent at the school door, assimilation occurring under expectation-laden institutions—was pressed consistently but B's parent-self-interest and multilingual-institutions responses kept it contested rather than decisive. B's closing crystallized the weighing better; A's closing largely restated the one-way-deal frame. Minor ding to B for claiming the key question "was never answered" when A had addressed it, but B then engaged the actual answer. Clear but competitive edge to CON.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B2.1: catching that A had relabeled opportunity as "expectation doing its work," then converting that concession into the persistent social-expectation-vs-formal-gate dichotomy that B rode through B4.5 and the closing. A's best recovery was A2.4—that workplaces teach the language only because they can require it, and that subsidized indefinite translation makes remaining outside costless—but B's symmetry and gate-cost weighing ultimately blunted it.</best_rebuttal>
